label: Person
name: Styrbjörn the Strong
summary:
Styrbjörn the Strong was, according to late Norse sagas, a son of the Swedish king Olof Björnsson and nephew of Eric the Victorious, who defeated and killed Styrbjörn at the Battle of Fyrisvellir (c. 985 CE). Though his historicity is uncertain, Styrbjörn appears in multiple independent Norse sources and is likely based on a real Viking-age figure whose exploits were remembered through oral tradition.

According to the Styrbjarnar þáttr Svíakappa and associated sagas, Styrbjörn was dispossessed of the Swedish throne by his uncle Eric after his father's death, and became a mercenary war-leader in the Baltic. He commanded the Jomsvikings — the legendary Norse warrior brotherhood based at Jomsborg on the south Baltic coast — and invaded Sweden with a large fleet supported by Harald Bluetooth of Denmark. Eric the Victorious defeated him decisively at Fyrisvellir near Uppsala, allegedly through a bargain with Odin (he sacrificed himself to the god for victory).

Styrbjörn's story represents one of the best-documented episodes of late Viking-age Scandinavian power politics and is important for understanding the transition from the Viking period to the consolidation of the Scandinavian kingdoms. His defeat helped secure Swedish royal centralization under Eric. A rune stone at Hässleby (Sweden) has been interpreted as commemorating him. The story influenced later Scandinavian literary tradition and modern retellings of Viking history.
